title: Section 133 CrPC in Bangladesh: Boundary Wall, Drainage & Public Nuisance Guide
metaTitle: Section 133 CrPC in Bangladesh: Boundary & Drainage Disputes
metaDescription: Resolve neighbor boundary disputes, illegal road obstruction, and drainage nuisance under Section 133 CrPC before Executive Magistrates in Bangladesh.
heroIntro: In both densely populated urban neighborhoods of Dhaka and rural village homesteads across Bangladesh, conflicts between adjacent property owners frequently escalate over blocked drainage lines, unauthorized boundary walls, and obstructed access pathways. When an uncooperative neighbor unlawfully builds a brick wall across a shared road, redirects toxic sewage runoff into an adjacent compound, or constructs a hazardous structural overhang that threatens collapse, victims face an immediate threat to health, safety, and property value. While filing an easement suit in a civil court can take years, the **Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC)** provides a rapid, summary legal remedy under **Section 133**. Empowering Executive Magistrates to issue conditional orders for the immediate removal of public nuisances and illegal obstructions, Section 133 is one of the most effective community dispute resolution tools in Bangladesh. This practical legal guide by Advocate Md. Shah Alam, Supreme Court Advocate and property law practitioner in Uttara and Dhaka Court, explains how to petition the Executive Magistrate, enforce municipal demolition orders, and protect neighborhood rights.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Overview: How Section 133 CrPC Resolves Neighbor and Nuisance Disputes
quickAnswer.heading: Quick Overview: How Section 133 CrPC Resolves Neighbor and Nuisance Disputes
quickAnswer.text: Under Section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC), an Executive Magistrate (such as an Additional District Magistrate or Upazila Nirbahi Officer) possesses statutory authority to issue an emergency Conditional Order directing the removal of any unlawful obstruction or nuisance from any way, river, or channel lawfully used by the public. When an aggrieved citizen files a petition regarding a blocked pathway, illegal wall, or hazardous drainage discharge, the Magistrate issues a conditional order requiring the person causing the nuisance to remove it within a fixed timeframe (typically 7 to 14 days) or appear in court to show cause under Section 135. If the respondent denies the existence of a public right, the Magistrate conducts an inquiry under Section 139A. If reliable evidence supporting the denial is absent, or if the nuisance is established, the order is made absolute under Section 137, empowering local police or municipal authorities to demolish the obstruction.

sections.title: 1. Statutory Foundation: Public Nuisance Powers Under Chapter X CrPC
sections.content:
In Bangladesh, while private boundary encroachments between two individuals can be resolved through civil boundary suits, actions that compromise public health, common pathways, sanitation, and neighborhood safety fall within the criminal public nuisance jurisdiction codified in Chapter X of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 (CrPC).

Under Section 133 of the CrPC, Parliament vested summary administrative and quasi-judicial authority in Executive Magistrates (specifically the Additional District Magistrate in metropolitan cities and Upazila Nirbahi Officers in rural upazilas) to order the immediate cessation or demolition of public nuisances. The section is not punitive; it is preventive and remedial, aimed at swiftly restoring public convenience and safety before civil litigation can unfold.

The statutory definition of a public nuisance is linked to Section 268 of the Penal Code 1860: an act or omission that causes common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity. Because Section 133 proceedings are swift, cost-effective, and backed by direct police enforcement, they are widely utilized by citizens facing unyielding neighbors and illegal construction cartels.

sections.title: 2. Actionable Nuisances: Blocked Roads, Boundary Walls & Drainage
sections.content:
Section 133(1) of the CrPC identifies specific categories of actionable public nuisances that empower an Executive Magistrate to intervene:

  • Unlawful Obstruction of Public Ways: Any unauthorized construction of a brick wall, bamboo barricade, iron gate, or earth filling that narrows or completely blocks any public road, shared lane, alleyway, or village pathway lawfully used by the public.
  • Illegal Drainage and Sewage Discharges: Redirecting household sewage, septic overflow, or contaminated factory chemical wastewater into neighboring private compounds, public surface drains, or open roads, creating grave public health hazards.
  • Dangerous Structural Overhangs: Old, dilapidated walls, unapproved building projections, decaying concrete parapets, or tilted structures adjoining a public street that threaten imminent collapse on passersby.
  • Noxious Occupations & Industrial Hazards: Operating unauthorized chemical storage facilities, illegal tanneries, noisy industrial workshops, or hazardous sawmills in residential zones in violation of zoning regulations.
  • Unenclosed Wells and Excavations: Leaving deep construction excavations, open water wells, or quarry pits unfenced near public thoroughfares.

sections.title: 3. The Conditional Order Mechanism Under Section 133(1)
sections.content:
When an aggrieved citizen or neighborhood community submits a petition under Section 133, accompanied by a police report or personal affidavit, the Executive Magistrate does not immediately issue a final demolition order. The statute enforces strict procedural due process through a Conditional Order.

Under Section 133(1), the Magistrate issues an order directing the person causing the obstruction or nuisance, within a fixed time to be specified in the order:

  1. To remove such obstruction or nuisance; or
  2. To desist from carrying on, or to remove or regulate such trade or occupation; or
  3. To repair, support, or remove such dangerous building or structure; or
  4. The Show Cause Option: If they object to doing so, to appear before the Magistrate at a fixed time and place to show cause why the conditional order should not be made absolute.

Under Section 134, the conditional order is officially served on the respondent in the manner provided for serving a summons, or by public notice posted at the site of the nuisance.

sections.title: 4. Section 139A Procedure: Denying the Existence of a Public Right
sections.content:
Dealing with an obstructed pathway, illegal boundary wall, or drainage nuisance? Contact our land litigation chamber on WhatsApp at +880 1955-802007, or call +880 1712-655546. We coordinate magistrate petitions and police reports.

When an obstruction concerns a pathway, road, or water channel, the respondent frequently appears and argues that the land is private property and that no public right exists. To resolve this threshold challenge, the CrPC provides a mandatory statutory mechanism: Section 139A.

Under Section 139A, the Magistrate must follow a two-tier inquiry:

  • Questioning the Respondent: The Magistrate must specifically ask the respondent whether they deny the existence of any public right in respect of the way, river, or channel.
  • Inquiry into Reliable Evidence: If the respondent denies the public right, the Magistrate must inquire into the matter before proceeding further. The respondent must produce reliable evidence (such as original title deeds, CS/RS/BS Khatians showing private ownership without public easement notations) supporting their denial.
  • Outcome of the Inquiry: If the Magistrate finds there is reliable evidence supporting the denial, the court must stay all proceedings until the matter of public right is decided by a competent civil court. If, however, the respondent produces no reliable evidence or merely raises frivolous objections, the Magistrate rejects the denial and proceeds with the nuisance inquiry under Section 137.

sections.title: 6. The Role of Police Spot Reports & Municipal Engineer Inspections
sections.content:
When a Section 133 proceeding is initiated, the Executive Magistrate directs institutional field investigations to ascertain the ground reality:

  1. Police Station Spot Report (Todontoprotibedon): The local police station Officer-in-Charge directs an investigating officer to visit the locus in quo. The officer prepares an on-site sketch map (Noksha), records statements from neighboring residents, examines whether public access has been interrupted, and reports whether the obstruction poses an imminent public hazard.
  2. Municipal or Union Parishad Inspection: In urban areas (such as Dhaka City Corporation or Gazipur City Corporation), the Magistrate calls for an inspection report from the City Corporation Zonal Executive Officer or Assistant Engineer. The municipal engineer verifies approved master plan roads, official drainage lines, and determines whether the structure violates building setbacks.

Securing an accurate, photographic spot report is the single most critical factor in achieving a successful Section 133 order. An advocate guides the client in providing municipal road maps and photographic evidence directly to the investigating officers.

sections.title: 7. Making the Order Absolute & Criminal Penalties Under Section 188
sections.content:
If the respondent appears and shows cause against the conditional order, the Magistrate proceeds to take evidence in the matter as in a summons case under Section 137 of the CrPC.

The legal transition to final enforcement involves:

  • Making the Order Absolute (Section 137(3)): If the Magistrate is satisfied that the conditional order is reasonable and proper, the order is made Absolute. The Magistrate delivers a formal judgment commanding the respondent to perform the specified act (e.g. demolish the wall or clear the drain) within a fixed deadline.
  • Criminal Penalty Under Section 188 Penal Code: Under Section 136 and Section 140 of the CrPC, if the respondent fails to perform the act within the time specified in an absolute order, they become liable to the criminal penalties prescribed in Section 188 of the Penal Code 1860 (Disobedience to an order duly promulgated by a public servant), punishable with imprisonment up to six months and fines.
  • Criminal Revision Before Sessions Judge: An aggrieved party against whom an absolute order is passed can challenge the legality by filing a Criminal Revision under Section 435/439A CrPC before the Sessions Judge Court.

sections.title: 8. Demolition Protocol & Recovering Costs from the Offender
sections.content:
A uniquely powerful dimension of Section 133 is that the court does not rely on the goodwill of the offender to carry out demolition. Under Section 140 of the CrPC, if the absolute order is not obeyed within the specified time, the Magistrate may cause the act to be performed directly by state machinery.

The statutory enforcement mechanism operates as follows:

  1. Direction to Police and Municipal Authorities: The Magistrate issues a formal demolition requisition to the local Police Station and City Corporation / Pourashava engineering department.
  2. State-Supervised Demolition: Law enforcement personnel and municipal demolition crews enter the land, tear down the illegal brick wall, clear the obstructed drainage ditch, or dismantle the hazardous structure under police protection.
  3. Recovery of Demolition Expenses: Under Section 140(2), the entire financial cost incurred by the government in carrying out the demolition may be recovered from the offender either by the sale of any building materials removed, or by the distress and sale of any other movable property belonging to the offender as if it were a fine.

sections.title: 9. Illustrative Scenario: Removing an Illegal Wall Blocking a Pathway in Dhaka
sections.content:
Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): In an established residential sector in Uttara, Dhaka, a 12-foot wide shared access road had been utilized by ten residential households for over thirty years to connect to the main avenue. An influential local plot owner purchased a corner parcel and constructed a 7-foot brick boundary wall extending 6 feet into the shared road, preventing emergency ambulances and vehicles from reaching neighboring houses, and severing the underground surface drainage pipe.

Facing intolerable nuisance and stagnant sewage flooding, the affected residents retained Advocate Md. Shah Alam's chamber. Our legal team launched a decisive Section 133 action:

  1. Drafted and filed an emergency petition under Section 133 CrPC before the Court of the Additional District Magistrate (ADM), Dhaka, submitting historical layout maps, City Corporation tax holding records, and photographs of the blocked passage and sewage overflow.
  2. The ADM issued an immediate Conditional Order directing the plot owner to demolish the wall within 10 days or show cause, while directing the local police station to submit an emergency Spot Report.
  3. Accompanied the police Sub-Inspector during the on-site inquiry, presenting statements from eight neighborhood residents confirming continuous public use of the road for three decades.
  4. When the plot owner appeared and claimed under Section 139A that the road was his private land, our advocates demonstrated that his own purchase deed referenced the 12-foot shared boundary road, disproving any reliable evidence of private ownership.
  5. The ADM rejected the Section 139A objection and made the conditional order Absolute under Section 137. When the owner failed to demolish the wall within 7 days, the Magistrate dispatched municipal bulldozers and police personnel under Section 140, completely demolishing the illegal wall, restoring the drainage line, and recovering all demolition costs from the offender.

faqs.question: What is Section 133 of the CrPC in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Section 133 CrPC is an emergency statutory mechanism empowering Executive Magistrates to issue conditional orders for the swift removal of public nuisances, blocked pathways, and hazardous drainage discharges.

faqs.question: Which court hears public nuisance cases under Section 133?
faqs.answer: Section 133 petitions are heard by the Court of the Additional District Magistrate (ADM) in metropolitan districts or Upazila Nirbahi Officers (UNO) in rural upazilas.

faqs.question: What happens if a neighbor denies that a pathway is a public road?
faqs.answer: Under Section 139A CrPC, the Magistrate inquires whether reliable evidence supports the denial. If reliable evidence exists, proceedings are stayed for civil court determination; if absent, the nuisance inquiry proceeds.

faqs.question: Can the magistrate order the demolition of an illegal wall under Section 133?
faqs.answer: Yes. If the conditional order is made absolute under Section 137 and the offender fails to remove it, the magistrate can direct police and municipal bulldozers to demolish the wall under Section 140 CrPC.

faqs.question: Who pays for the cost of demolishing an illegal obstruction under Section 140?
faqs.answer: Under Section 140(2) CrPC, all expenses incurred by the government in executing the demolition are recovered directly from the offender through the distress and sale of their property.

faqs.question: What is the penalty for disobeying a final order under Section 133?
faqs.answer: Disobeying an absolute order under Section 133 CrPC constitutes a criminal offence under Section 188 of the Penal Code 1860, punishable with simple imprisonment up to six months and fines.

faqs.question: Can private drainage overflow be resolved under Section 133?
faqs.answer: Yes. Discharging contaminated sewage or wastewater onto neighboring land or shared alleys creates a public health nuisance directly actionable under Section 133 CrPC.

faqs.question: Can an overseas property owner file a Section 133 petition from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. An expatriate landowner whose property access is blocked in Bangladesh can file a Section 133 petition through an advocate or authorized local power of attorney.
